title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
Cline's automated issue triage system used Claude AI to respond to GitHub issues without human review of the AI's outputs. An attacker could inject malicious instructions into issue text that would cause Claude to execute arbitrary code. This prompt injection vulnerability existed in a system designed to handle untrusted user input, which is exactly where such attacks are most dangerous.

The vulnerability created a path to compromise Cline's software releases. An attacker who successfully exploited the issue triage system could use GitHub Actions cache poisoning to steal publishing credentials and upload malicious versions to package repositories used by millions of developers. The attack was discoverable through basic security testing of the issue triage workflow against adversarial inputs, and preventable through human review of Claude's responses before execution.

The researcher reported the vulnerability through official channels but received no response for over a month. It is not established whether the vulnerability was actually exploited in production to compromise releases, though evidence suggests an exploitation attempt may have occurred.

summary:
Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, had a critical security vulnerability between December 21, 2025, and February 9, 2026. Researcher Adnan Khan discovered that Cline's automated issue triage workflow, which used Claude AI to respond to GitHub issues, was susceptible to prompt injection attacks. Any user could open an issue with malicious instructions that would trick Claude into executing arbitrary code. An attacker could then exploit GitHub Actions cache poisoning to steal publishing credentials and compromise Cline releases across Visual Studio Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM.

Khan reported the vulnerability through official channels starting January 1st but received no response from the Cline team. He published his findings publicly on February 9th, prompting an immediate fix within one hour. Cline removed the vulnerable workflows and rotated all affected credentials. While there was evidence someone may have attempted exploitation and possibly obtained valid credentials, no malicious updates were confirmed. Users were advised to disable auto-updates until Cline verified no unauthorized access occurred.
